name: Cardiovascular System
summary:
Every cell in your body is a small, demanding city. It needs fuel, oxygen, and a way to throw out waste, and it needs these things every minute of every day. The cardiovascular system is the delivery service that makes that possible: a heart that never stops pumping, a tree of arteries that carries blood outward, a web of capillaries where goods are exchanged, and a set of veins that brings the blood home. Laid end to end, your blood vessels would stretch roughly 100,000 kilometers, enough to circle the planet more than twice.

The system runs two loops at once. In the pulmonary circuit, the right side of the heart sends oxygen-poor blood to the lungs and receives it back refreshed. In the systemic circuit, the left side pushes that refreshed blood through the aorta to the brain, muscles, skin, and organs. Valves keep traffic one-way, and elastic walls keep pressure steady between beats. Together, the loops move about 5 liters of blood around your body, roughly a gallon, in about a minute.

What makes it remarkable is the tuning. Arterioles widen and narrow to send blood where it is needed, capillaries slow the flow so oxygen can cross, and veins hold most of your blood in reserve. When you sprint, the system redirects. When you sleep, it eases back.
functions: Delivers oxygen and nutrients to every cell in the body
Carries carbon dioxide and other waste away from tissues
Distributes hormones and immune cells through the bloodstream
Keeps blood pressure steady enough to perfuse the brain
Helps regulate body temperature by rerouting blood flow

organs.name: Heart
organs.tagline: A tireless four-chambered pump the size of your fist.
organs.summary:
Your heart sits in the middle of your chest, tucked between your lungs and tipped slightly to the left. It is about the size of your closed fist and weighs roughly 300 grams (about 10 ounces). A tough sac called the pericardium wraps it, and four chambers hide inside: two small atria on top that receive blood, and two muscular ventricles below that push it out. Valves between them snap shut with every beat, making the familiar lub-dub.

Blood enters the right atrium from your body, drops to the right ventricle, and travels to your lungs for oxygen. It returns to the left atrium, then the left ventricle drives it into the aorta and out to every tissue you have. The left ventricle's wall is three times thicker than the right's because it pushes against the whole body's resistance. No pause, no shift change: this four-chambered pump repeats the cycle about 100,000 times a day, for your entire life.

functions.title: Pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs
functions.detail: The right side collects returning blood and sends it to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.

functions.title: Drives oxygen-rich blood to the body
functions.detail: The left ventricle forces blood into the aorta with enough pressure to reach your brain, toes, and fingertips.

functions.title: Keeps two circuits separate
functions.detail: A four-valve design stops fresh and used blood from mixing, so each circuit gets the blood it needs.

functions.title: Sets the rhythm
functions.detail: A tiny patch of specialized muscle, the sinoatrial node, fires electrical signals that keep the chambers beating in order.

organs.location: In the center of the chest, behind the sternum and between the lungs, with its lower tip angled toward the left.
organs.size: About the size of a closed fist, roughly 12 cm (4.7 in) long and 250 to 350 g (9 to 12 oz) in adults.
facts: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day, close to 3 billion times over an average lifetime.
The heart's own supply comes from the coronary arteries, which branch off the aorta just above the aortic valve.
At rest, an adult heart moves about 5 liters of blood every minute, roughly the body's entire blood volume.

conditions.name: Coronary artery disease
conditions.description: Plaque builds up inside the arteries that feed the heart muscle, narrowing them and limiting blood flow during exertion.

conditions.name: Heart failure
conditions.description: The heart cannot pump strongly enough to meet the body's needs, so fluid can collect in the lungs and legs.

conditions.name: Arrhythmia
conditions.description: The heart's electrical signals fall out of step, making beats too fast, too slow, or irregular.

organs.name: Aorta
organs.tagline: The body's main highway, built to stretch with every beat.
organs.summary:
The aorta is the body's main highway, a thick elastic pipe about 2.5 to 3 cm (1 to 1.2 in) wide that leaves the left ventricle and arches over the heart like a cane handle. From there it descends through the chest and abdomen, tucked just in front of the spine, before splitting into two iliac arteries near your navel. Its wall is packed with elastic fibers and smooth muscle, built to handle the highest pressure in your circulation.

Every heartbeat sends a wave of blood into the aorta, and its stretchy wall absorbs the surge, then recoils to keep blood moving between beats. Along the way, branches peel off to feed your brain, arms, kidneys, gut, and legs. Because the aorta carries so much pressure, its wall can balloon into an aneurysm or tear into a dissection, both of which are serious. Think of it as the trunk of a tree that every other artery grows from.

functions.title: Carries the full output of the heart
functions.detail: Every stroke of the left ventricle enters the aorta, which distributes roughly 5 liters a minute to the body at rest.

functions.title: Smooths the pulse
functions.detail: Elastic fibers stretch during each beat and recoil between beats, keeping blood moving even when the valve is closed.

functions.title: Feeds the head and arms
functions.detail: Branches from the arch, including the carotid and subclavian arteries, supply the brain and upper limbs.

functions.title: Supplies the abdomen and legs
functions.detail: Along its descent it gives off arteries to the kidneys, liver, gut, and eventually the legs.

organs.location: It begins at the left ventricle, arches over the heart, and descends through the chest and abdomen in front of the spine.
organs.size: About 2.5 to 3 cm (1 to 1.2 in) across at its widest, roughly the width of a quarter.
facts: The aorta is about as wide as a quarter, roughly 2.5 to 3 cm (1 to 1.2 in) across.
It is not straight: it rises, arches like a cane handle, then descends behind the heart.
Its elastic wall stores energy with each beat and releases it between beats, smoothing the pulse.

conditions.name: Aortic aneurysm
conditions.description: A weak section of the aortic wall balloons outward, and a large one can rupture, which is life-threatening.

conditions.name: Aortic dissection
conditions.description: A tear in the inner lining lets blood burrow into the wall, splitting its layers apart.

conditions.name: Coarctation of the aorta
conditions.description: A congenital narrowing of the aorta forces the heart to pump harder to push blood past it.

organs.name: Coronary Arteries
organs.tagline: The heart's own fuel lines, only millimeters wide.
organs.summary:
Your heart is a muscle that works every second, and like any muscle it needs its own blood supply. Two coronary arteries, the left and the right, branch off the aorta just above the aortic valve and wrap around the heart's surface like a crown, which is what coronary means. The left one quickly splits into two main branches that run down the front and around the side; the right circles toward the back. Most are only 3 to 4 mm wide.

These small vessels deliver oxygen and fuel to the working muscle and carry carbon dioxide away. When you climb stairs, they widen to meet the extra demand. Plaque can narrow them, so the muscle complains with chest pain during exertion, and a sudden clot can block one entirely, starving a patch of heart muscle. That is why doctors call the coronary arteries the heart's own lifeline.

functions.title: Nourish the heart muscle
functions.detail: They deliver oxygen and fuel to the myocardium, which cannot absorb oxygen from the blood inside its own chambers.

functions.title: Branch into a fine network
functions.detail: The left artery divides into two main branches, and smaller vessels penetrate the muscle to reach every fiber.

functions.title: Adjust flow to demand
functions.detail: During exercise the coronary arteries widen, sometimes increasing flow several times to match a faster heartbeat.

functions.title: Supply the conduction system
functions.detail: Small branches feed the nodes and fibers that carry electrical signals, helping keep the rhythm reliable.

organs.location: They branch from the aortic root and run along the outer surface of the heart, dipping into the muscle.
organs.size: Main branches are typically 3 to 4 mm wide, with smaller branches tapering to less than a millimeter.
facts: Coronary arteries are only about 3 to 4 mm wide, narrower than a drinking straw.
The heart cannot use the oxygen in the blood inside its chambers; it depends on these vessels instead.
The coronary arteries receive roughly 5 percent of the heart's output at rest, though the heart is less than 1 percent of body weight.

conditions.name: Coronary artery disease
conditions.description: Plaque narrows the coronary arteries, so the heart muscle receives less blood than it needs, especially during exertion.

conditions.name: Angina
conditions.description: Chest pressure or tightness appears when a narrowed coronary artery cannot keep up with the heart's demand for oxygen.

conditions.name: Heart attack
conditions.description: A clot blocks a coronary artery and a section of heart muscle begins to die from lack of oxygen.

organs.name: Arteries
organs.tagline: Outbound roads that carry oxygen to every tissue.
organs.summary:
Arteries are the outbound lanes of your circulation: muscular, elastic tubes that carry blood away from the heart and branch into smaller and smaller roads. A large artery has three layers, an inner lining of smooth cells, a thick middle layer of muscle and elastic fibers, and an outer coat of connective tissue. That middle layer is why arteries hold their round shape even when empty and can tighten or relax to change blood flow.

As arteries travel outward, they narrow into arterioles, the tiny adjustable taps that decide which tissues get blood right now. During a meal, your gut arterioles widen; during a sprint, your leg muscles win. This constant tuning is a major reason blood pressure stays stable. One quirk: not every artery carries oxygen-rich blood. The pulmonary arteries are the exception, carrying used blood from the heart to the lungs.

functions.title: Carry blood away from the heart
functions.detail: They form the outbound half of the circulation, delivering oxygen and nutrients to tissues throughout the body.

functions.title: Maintain pressure between beats
functions.detail: Elastic walls recoil after each surge, keeping blood pressure from falling to zero before the next beat.

functions.title: Control where blood goes
functions.detail: Arterioles, the smallest arteries, widen or narrow to redirect flow toward muscles, skin, or digestive organs.

functions.title: Hold their shape
functions.detail: A thick middle layer of muscle and elastic fiber keeps arteries round and resists the stress of high pressure.

organs.location: They begin at the aorta and branch through every region of the body, from the neck to the toes.
organs.size: The largest, like the aorta, reach 2.5 to 3 cm across, while small arteries narrow to about 1 mm.
facts: Arteries have thicker, more muscular walls than veins because they carry blood at much higher pressure.
The smallest arteries, arterioles, can change diameter to redirect blood and help set blood pressure.
The pulmonary arteries are the only arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood.

conditions.name: Atherosclerosis
conditions.description: Fatty plaque builds up in artery walls, narrowing the channel and stiffening the vessel over time.

conditions.name: High blood pressure
conditions.description: Persistently high pressure strains artery walls and makes them more likely to stiffen or suffer damage.

conditions.name: Peripheral artery disease
conditions.description: Narrowed arteries in the legs limit blood flow, often causing cramping pain during walking.

organs.name: Veins
organs.tagline: Low-pressure return lanes with one-way valves.
organs.summary:
Veins are the return lanes. Their walls are thinner and floppier than arteries because the blood inside arrives at low pressure, and many of them carry one-way valves that keep blood from sliding backward. Superficial veins run just under your skin, which is why you can see blue-green lines on your wrist; deep veins travel beside the major arteries. The largest, the vena cava, empties into the right atrium.

Roughly 60 to 70 percent of your blood sits in your veins at any moment, making them the body's quiet reservoir. They do not have a pump of their own, so they borrow yours: when leg muscles squeeze, they milk blood upward, and valves catch it between squeezes. Breathing helps too, pulling blood toward the chest. Stand still for a long time and that system struggles, which is why your feet can feel heavy.

functions.title: Return blood to the heart
functions.detail: They collect oxygen-poor blood from tissues and carry it back toward the right atrium.

functions.title: Keep flow one-way
functions.detail: One-way valves, especially in the legs, prevent blood from sliding backward when you stand still.

functions.title: Store most of your blood
functions.detail: Veins hold roughly 60 to 70 percent of total blood volume, acting as a reservoir the body can tap when needed.

functions.title: Borrow the muscle pump
functions.detail: Squeezing leg muscles during walking pushes blood upward, while breathing helps pull it toward the chest.

organs.location: They run throughout the body, with superficial veins under the skin and deep veins alongside the major arteries.
organs.size: They range from tiny venules under a millimeter to the vena cava at about 2.5 cm (1 in) across.
facts: Veins hold roughly 60 to 70 percent of your blood at any moment, making them the body's main reservoir.
Veins look blue through skin because of how light scatters, not because the blood inside is blue.
If a vein valve weakens, blood can pool and the vein may bulge into a varicose vein.

conditions.name: Varicose veins
conditions.description: Weakened valves let blood pool in a superficial vein, which stretches and twists visibly under the skin.

conditions.name: Deep vein thrombosis
conditions.description: A blood clot forms in a deep vein, usually in the leg, and can obstruct the return of blood.

conditions.name: Chronic venous insufficiency
conditions.description: Vein valves stop working well over time, leading to swelling, aching, and skin changes in the lower legs.

organs.name: Capillaries
organs.tagline: One-cell-thick vessels where blood meets tissue.
organs.summary:
Capillaries are where the circulation stops being plumbing and starts being chemistry. These are the smallest vessels in the body, most just 5 to 10 micrometers across, barely wider than a single red blood cell. Their walls are only one cell thick. Rather than running alone, they form dense webs called capillary beds inside almost every tissue, so close together that almost every cell sits within a tenth of a millimeter of one.

Here oxygen slips out of the blood and into cells, while carbon dioxide and waste slip in. The exchange happens by diffusion, driven by simple differences in concentration, and it needs no pump at all. Blood also slows to a crawl as it spreads through these vast, narrow networks, giving the swap time to finish. Then the capillaries merge into small veins, and the journey home begins. Your life depends on this quiet, microscopic handoff.

functions.title: Exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide
functions.detail: Oxygen diffuses out of the blood into cells while carbon dioxide diffuses in, all without any active pumping.

functions.title: Deliver nutrients and remove waste
functions.detail: Glucose, amino acids, and hormones cross into tissues, while metabolic waste enters the blood for disposal.

functions.title: Slow the blood
functions.detail: Their enormous combined width drops blood speed to a crawl, giving exchange time to happen.

functions.title: Connect arteries to veins
functions.detail: Capillary beds sit between arterioles and venules, completing the circuit from heart back to heart.

organs.location: They form dense networks inside nearly every tissue, bridging the smallest arteries and veins.
organs.size: Most are 5 to 10 micrometers wide, about the diameter of a single red blood cell.
facts: Most capillaries are 5 to 10 micrometers wide, so red blood cells pass through in single file, sometimes folding to fit.
Capillaries are so numerous that almost every cell in your body sits within about a tenth of a millimeter of one.
Blood slows dramatically in capillaries, giving oxygen and nutrients time to cross into tissues.

conditions.name: Edema
conditions.description: Fluid leaks from capillaries into surrounding tissue faster than it is drained, causing swelling in the affected area.

conditions.name: Diabetic retinopathy
conditions.description: High blood sugar damages the tiny capillaries of the retina, making them leak or bleed and threatening vision.

organs.name: Vena Cava
organs.tagline: Two great veins emptying into the right atrium.
organs.summary:
The vena cava is not one vessel but two. The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, arms, and chest, while the much larger inferior vena cava runs up the back of the abdomen beside the spine, collecting blood from the legs, kidneys, liver, and gut. Both empty into the right atrium of the heart. The inferior vena cava is the widest vein in your body, about 2.5 cm (1 in) across.

These are low-pressure pipes. Blood arriving through them is moving slowly, pushed by muscles, breathing, and the suction of the heart's relaxed atrium. Because the inferior vena cava is so wide and sits deep in the abdomen, a clot in a leg vein can travel into it, and pressure from a tumor or clot can back up into the organs below. Still, on an ordinary day, it quietly returns nearly every drop of blood you have.

functions.title: Drain the upper body
functions.detail: The superior vena cava collects blood from the head, neck, arms, and chest and empties it into the right atrium.

functions.title: Drain the lower body
functions.detail: The inferior vena cava carries blood from the legs, kidneys, liver, and gut back toward the heart.

functions.title: Act as a low-pressure reservoir
functions.detail: Their wide, thin walls let them hold a large volume of blood at pressures far below those in arteries.

functions.title: Work with breathing and muscles
functions.detail: Pressure changes in the chest and squeezing by surrounding muscles help push blood upward through these veins.

organs.location: The superior vena cava runs down the right side of the upper chest; the inferior vena cava climbs the back of the abdomen.
organs.size: The inferior vena cava is about 2.5 cm (1 in) wide, making it the largest vein in the body.
facts: The inferior vena cava is the largest vein in the body, about 2.5 cm (1 in) across.
The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, arms, and chest, while the inferior drains everything below the diaphragm.
Blood returning from your feet passes through the inferior vena cava before reaching the heart.

conditions.name: Superior vena cava syndrome
conditions.description: A clot or tumor presses on the superior vena cava, blocking drainage from the head and arms and causing swelling.

conditions.name: Deep vein thrombosis
conditions.description: A clot that forms in a deep leg vein can extend toward the inferior vena cava and obstruct the return of blood.

organs.name: Pulmonary Arteries
organs.tagline: The only arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood.
organs.summary:
The pulmonary arteries are the great exception in your circulation. Most arteries carry oxygen-rich blood away from the heart, but these carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. They begin as a single short, wide trunk, about 5 cm long and 3 cm across, which splits into a right and left artery, one for each lung. Inside the lungs they branch alongside the airways, shrinking until they become capillary nets around the air sacs.

Because the lungs are close to the heart and their delicate air sacs cannot take high pressure, this circuit runs at roughly a fifth of aortic pressure. That is enough to push blood through the lungs in a couple of seconds, just long enough to pick up oxygen and drop off carbon dioxide. Oxygen-rich blood then returns to the left atrium through the pulmonary veins, ready for the next trip around the body.

functions.title: Carry blood to the lungs
functions.detail: They move oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the capillary beds around the air sacs.

functions.title: Keep lung pressure low
functions.detail: Thin walls and low resistance protect delicate air sacs while still moving the whole cardiac output.

functions.title: Split for each lung
functions.detail: The short pulmonary trunk divides into right and left arteries, which follow the airways deep into each lung.

functions.title: Set up the return trip
functions.detail: After gas exchange, blood drains into pulmonary veins and returns to the left atrium, ready for the body.

organs.location: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle and splits into right and left pulmonary arteries at about the level of the upper chest.
organs.size: The trunk is roughly 5 cm (2 in) long and 3 cm (1.2 in) wide before it divides.
facts: Pulmonary arteries are the only arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood.
The pulmonary trunk is only about 5 cm (2 in) long and 3 cm (1.2 in) wide before it splits.
Pressure in the pulmonary arteries is roughly a fifth of the pressure in the aorta, protecting the lungs' delicate air sacs.

conditions.name: Pulmonary embolism
conditions.description: A clot lodges in a pulmonary artery, blocking blood flow to part of a lung and reducing oxygen uptake.

conditions.name: Pulmonary arterial hypertension
conditions.description: The small pulmonary arteries thicken and narrow, raising pressure in the lung circuit and straining the right ventricle.

conditions.name: Pulmonary stenosis
conditions.description: A narrowed pulmonary valve forces the right ventricle to work harder to push blood toward the lungs.

lesson.title: Follow the blood: a tour of circulation
lesson.subtitle: Trace a single drop of blood from your heart to your toes and back again.

steps.title: A knock at the wrist
steps.body: Put two fingers on the inside of your wrist and wait. There it is, a small, steady knock that has been happening since before you were born. That knock is the sound of pressure arriving, the front edge of a wave of blood pushed out by a pump roughly the size of your fist. In the next few minutes, follow one drop of that blood all the way around: out through the arteries, through the tiniest vessels you have, and back through the veins. By the end, the number at your wrist will mean something different. Ready?
steps.keyPoint: A pulse is pressure you can feel, arriving with every heartbeat.

steps.title: Two pumps in one
steps.body: Your heart is two pumps bolted together. The right side collects blood that has already delivered its oxygen and sends it to the lungs. The left side takes the refreshed blood back and drives it out to the body. Each side has an upper chamber, the atrium, that receives, and a lower chamber, the ventricle, that pushes. Valves between them close with each beat, which is the lub-dub you hear through a stethoscope. Notice the left ventricle's wall: it is much thicker, because it has the harder job. Follow the blood it just launched.
steps.keyPoint: The left ventricle is thicker because it pumps against the resistance of the whole body.

steps.title: The detour to the lungs
steps.body: From the right ventricle, blood leaves through the pulmonary arteries, the only arteries in your body that carry oxygen-poor blood. They rise a short distance and split, one branch to each lung, then keep dividing until they wrap around millions of tiny air sacs. There the blood gives up carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen. The walls here are thin and the pressure is low, because the lungs are delicate. In a few seconds, the same drop is oxygen-rich and heading back to the left side of the heart. Now it is ready for the long trip.
steps.keyPoint: This is the one place where an artery carries used, oxygen-poor blood.

steps.title: Out through the trunk
steps.body: The left ventricle slams blood into the aorta, the widest artery you have, about the width of a quarter. It rises, arches over the heart like a cane handle, then descends through your chest and abdomen in front of the spine. Its wall is packed with elastic fibers, so it stretches with each surge and recoils between beats, smoothing the pulse into a steadier flow. Branches peel off along the way to the brain, arms, kidneys, and gut. Think of a tree trunk with a road leaving for every neighborhood.
steps.keyPoint: The aorta is a pressure reservoir, not just a pipe.

steps.title: The heart feeds itself
steps.body: Here is a puzzle: the heart is full of blood, but it cannot use any of it. The muscle wall is far too thick for oxygen to diffuse in from the chamber blood. So the heart feeds itself through the coronary arteries, two small vessels that branch off the aorta just above the aortic valve and wrap around the muscle like a crown. They are only a few millimeters wide. When you climb stairs, they widen to meet the demand. When plaque narrows them, that demand becomes chest pain. The heart, in other words, is its own most demanding customer.
steps.keyPoint: A muscle that never rests needs a blood supply that never stops.

steps.title: Where the handoff happens
steps.body: The aorta branches into arteries, arteries into arterioles, and arterioles into capillaries, vessels so narrow that red blood cells pass in single file. Their walls are one cell thick. This is where the real business happens: oxygen diffuses out, carbon dioxide diffuses in, and nutrients cross into tissues. Blood slows here on purpose, giving the exchange time. Every tissue you have, from retina to toenail, holds a dense web of these tiny tubes. It is less like a pipe and more like a marketplace, with goods crossing in both directions.
steps.keyPoint: Capillaries trade speed for contact, slowing blood so oxygen can cross.

steps.title: The road home
steps.body: Now the blood turns homeward. Capillaries merge into venules, then veins, which widen as they climb. Veins are thin-walled and low-pressure, so many of them carry one-way valves that stop blood from sliding back down. Your leg muscles help: each step squeezes the veins and milks blood upward, while breathing lowers pressure in your chest and pulls it along. The largest veins, the superior and inferior vena cava, empty into the right atrium. And just like that, the drop is back where it started. This is also why a long flight can leave your ankles feeling puffy.
steps.keyPoint: Your veins have no pump, so they borrow your muscles and your breath.

steps.title: One loop, endlessly
steps.body: One loop, two circuits, and a lifetime of repetitions. Blood leaves the left ventricle through the aorta, reaches the tissues through arteries and capillaries, and returns through veins and the vena cava to the right atrium. The right ventricle sends it to the lungs and back to the left atrium. Four chambers, four valves, and a pressure difference keep it all moving one way. Next time you feel your pulse, you are feeling the aorta's elastic recoil. Explore the heart next, then the coronary arteries that keep it running. From there, the cycle begins again.
steps.keyPoint: Every drop of blood passes through your heart twice on each full circuit.

quiz.question: Which chamber pushes oxygen-rich blood into the aorta?
quiz.explanation: The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it must drive blood through the aorta to the entire body, while the right ventricle only sends blood to the nearby lungs.

quiz.question: Which vessels carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs?
quiz.explanation: The pulmonary arteries are the one exception to the rule that arteries carry oxygen-rich blood. They carry used blood to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen.

quiz.question: What are the smallest blood vessels, with walls only one cell thick?
quiz.explanation: Capillaries are 5 to 10 micrometers wide, barely wider than a red blood cell, and their one-cell-thick walls let oxygen and waste cross by diffusion.

quiz.question: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the wall of the right ventricle?
options: It holds more blood at rest
It receives blood from the lungs
It must push blood through the entire body
quiz.explanation: The left ventricle drives blood into the aorta against the resistance of the whole systemic circulation. The right ventricle only pushes blood through the nearby, low-pressure lungs.

quiz.question: What feature do most veins have that arteries mostly lack?
quiz.explanation: Because blood in veins travels at low pressure, one-way valves catch it and keep it from flowing backward. Weakened valves can lead to varicose veins.

quiz.question: Which vessel returns blood from the legs and abdomen to the right atrium?
quiz.explanation: The inferior vena cava runs up the back of the abdomen beside the spine and empties into the right atrium. The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, and arms.

quiz.question: Why do the coronary arteries branch off the aorta so close to the aortic valve?
options: To carry blood directly to the lungs
To supply the heart muscle with freshly oxygenated blood
To let blood bypass the capillaries
To keep pressure in the aorta lower
quiz.explanation: The heart cannot absorb oxygen from the blood inside its chambers. Coronary arteries branch from the aortic root so the working muscle receives oxygen-rich blood straight from the aorta.

quiz.question: Why is blood pressure much lower in the pulmonary arteries than in the aorta?
options: The right ventricle is larger than the left
The lungs need low pressure because their air sacs are delicate
Blood flows backward through the pulmonary circuit
quiz.explanation: The pulmonary circuit is short and its capillary beds in the lungs are thin-walled, so it runs at roughly a fifth of aortic pressure. High pressure there would damage the air sacs.
